teaser: She turns, her lips part, and the picture stops one breath before she speaks.
review_notes:
1881 sale in The Hague: 2 guilders plus 30 cents premium, bought by A. A. des Tombe; bequeathed to the Mauritshuis in 1902.
2018 research ('The Girl in the Spotlight'): background was a green curtain (glaze of indigo and weld) that has darkened; fine eyelashes found; pearl has no hook.
Suggestion that the 'pearl' is too large to be real and may be glass or polished tin.
Date is an estimate (about 1665); size about 44.5 x 39 cm.
Roughly 37 paintings attributed to Vermeer.

lesson.text: Someone has just said her name. That is how it feels. Her shoulders still face away, her head has swung around, and her mouth has opened a little. In half a second she will speak, or turn back. Vermeer stops the clock right here, and it has stayed stopped for more than 350 years.

Most portraits of the 1600s show people who have settled into a pose and know they will be stared at. This girl has not settled. A turn over the shoulder is something the body cannot hold for long, which is why the picture feels like a glance and not a sitting.
Everything that makes the moment feel alive is wet: the eyes, the lips, the pearl. Vermeer gave each of them a touch of pure light, and almost nothing else.

lesson.title: Three wet lights
lesson.text: The camera will stop at the three places where light sits on a moist or polished surface.

spots.title: The eyes
spots.text: Each eye has one white dot, placed on the same side. Those dots tell you where the window is, and they make the gaze feel aimed at you.

spots.title: The lips
spots.text: The lower lip carries small pale highlights, and a pink dot marks the corner of the mouth. Parted lips suggest breath, a word about to come.

spots.title: The pearl
spots.text: It is two main touches: a bright white comma at the top left and a soft gray reflection of her collar below. No outline, and no hook attaching it to the ear.

lesson.text: So the most famous pearl in painting is barely painted. Your eye supplies the sphere. Some specialists doubt it is a pearl at all: it would be enormous for a real one, and may show a drop of glass or polished tin, a cheaper imitation that was common then.

The blue of the headscarf is natural ultramarine, made by grinding lapis lazuli, a stone carried to Europe from mines in what is now Afghanistan. It was among the most expensive pigments a painter could buy.

We do not know who she is, and that is not an accident. The Dutch called this kind of picture a tronie: a study of a head, a costume or an expression, not a paid likeness of a particular person. The turban, exotic in Delft, belongs to the costume.

The black behind her has a secret. Research in 2018 showed that Vermeer painted a dark green curtain there, using a translucent glaze that has changed over the centuries until it lost its color and its folds. The same study found fine eyelashes too small for the eye to make out.
A tronie is not a portrait of somebody. It is a picture of a look, and that is why anyone can feel she is turning toward them.
Her skin has no hard edges anywhere. Find the place where the nose melts into the cheek without a line.

spots.title: The lost edge
spots.text: The lit side of the nose and the cheek beside it share the same light tone. Vermeer draws no boundary between them. Soft transitions like this make the face feel seen in air, not cut out.

lesson.text: Vermeer worked slowly in Delft and left only about 37 paintings. When he died in 1675, aged 43 and in debt, his name faded quickly. For two hundred years pictures like this one changed hands for small sums, sometimes under other painters' names.

The canvas is small, about 44.5 by 39 centimeters (17.5 by 15 inches), close to the size of a real head. Stand in front of it at the Mauritshuis in The Hague and she meets you at eye level, at the distance of a conversation.

In 1881 the painting came up at an auction in The Hague, dirty and unrecognized. A collector bought it for two guilders and thirty cents, about the price of a modest meal. He left it to the Mauritshuis in 1902.

quiz.question: What is a tronie?
options: A study of a head, costume or expression, not a portrait of a named person
A portrait ordered by a rich family
quiz.explanation: A tronie shows a type or a look, which is why the girl has no name.

quiz.question: How is the pearl painted?
options: With a careful outline and a gold hook
With two main touches of light and no outline
quiz.explanation: A white highlight and a soft reflection of the collar are enough for your eye to build a sphere.

quiz.question: What did the 2018 research discover about the dark background?
options: It was painted by a later restorer
It was once a dark green curtain
quiz.explanation: A green glaze has changed over time until the curtain disappeared.

quiz.question: Where does the blue of the headscarf come from?
quiz.explanation: Natural ultramarine was made from lapis lazuli, a very costly stone.

facts.text: The painting was bought in 1881 for about two guilders.
facts.explanation: It was dirty and unrecognized when a collector picked it up at auction in The Hague.

facts.text: We know the name of the girl who posed for Vermeer.
facts.explanation: Her identity is unknown, and the picture is a tronie, not a portrait of someone in particular.
